The View from SomewherePart I · The idea

Chapter 4

Frames that do not compose

Web edition. Figures 4.2 and 4.4 are live: set the six factors, and move the wolf fifth round the circle.

Start on a C and stack perfect fifths. A perfect fifth is the interval between two strings whose lengths stand as two to three, so the frequencies stand as 3:2: C to G, G to D, D to A, and on around the twelve notes of the keyboard. After twelve steps you are on a C again, seven octaves above the one you left, and an octave is a doubling of frequency. Twelve factors of 3/2 ought to equal seven factors of 2. Multiply them out: (32)12=5314414096=129.746…and27=128.(32)12=5314414096=129.746…and27=128. They differ by a factor of 312/219=1.01364, about one and a third percent. No fifth was out of tune. Each note agrees perfectly with its neighbor, and the C you arrive at is not the C you left.

Nothing was measured here, so no sampling error can be blamed, and no amount of care in tuning will help: 3m=2n has no solution in positive integers, because one side is odd and the other even. The miss is in the arithmetic of the loop. This chapter is about that kind of miss. It is a different kind from the one in Chapter 3, where the data did not fit a model that could have fitted, and the difference will matter for the rest of the book.

The same multiplication shows up in a ship’s log and on a currency screen, and I will show both. By the end the reader will be able to look at the conversion factors around a loop and say whether the loop can close, before anyone has collected a single observation. You will see why taking logarithms hands that question to the loop test already familiar from earlier chapters. We will see what a piano tuner, a navigator and an arbitrageur each do with the miss that remains. And we will see why we need all of this in Chapter 11, where the same question comes back in probabilistic form.

4.1Twelve fifths and seven octaves

Pitch is easiest to handle on a logarithmic scale, because stacking intervals multiplies frequency ratios and logarithms turn products into sums. Musicians use the cent, one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone, so that an octave is 1200 cents and a ratio r measures 1200log2⁡r cents. A pure fifth is 701.955 cents. Twelve of them make 8423.46 cents, and seven octaves make 8400. The gap is the Pythagorean comma, 23.46 cents, a little under a quarter of a semitone. Whether that counts as small is a matter of ear, but it is the whole error that a single wolf fifth will carry in a moment.

Figure 4.1 draws the walk. The notes sit on the circle of fifths, a clock face with twelve positions, and each pure fifth moves you one position clockwise. To make the miss visible, the radius of the path records how far the walk has drifted from a closed circle, at the rate of one twelfth of the comma per step. After twelve steps you are on the thirteenth note of the walk, B⁠♯, which is where C ought to be and is not. The scale bar fixes the units: the gap in the picture is 23.46 cents on the same scale as the bar for one semitone, so nothing is exaggerated.

The picture is a loop in the sense of Chapter 2: twelve nodes, twelve edges, one cycle. What goes around each edge is a number, the ratio 3/2 in the direction of travel, and the loop closes only if the product of those numbers around the cycle is the ratio you started with. Everything else in the chapter is a generalization of that sentence.

4.2When every place keeps its own units

In Chapters 1 to 3, two places that compared a number meant the same thing by it. A price at Alder and a price at Birch were both prices, in the same currency and the same unit. That is too generous, as the first book argued: people inherit their frames, and two of them can say the same words and mean different things. Here is the smallest version of that idea that has any mathematics in it.

Take one good, wheat, and the three towns Alder, Birch and Cedar, joined in a triangle by three roads: road 1 from Alder to Birch, road 2 from Birch to Cedar, road 3 from Cedar to Alder. Each town keeps its books in its own private unit. When two towns compare, each converts its own number into whatever unit is agreed for that road.

Build the structure from the bottom, because I will use it for the rest of the book. At each town put a copy of the real line, the numbers that town might hold. Call it the stalk at that town. At each road put another copy of the real line, the space in which the two ends compare. Each town sends its number into each of its roads by a linear map, the restriction map, and on a copy of the real line a linear map is multiplication by a number. On road e from u to v, town u multiplies by ae and town v multiplies by be (Figure 4.2). A shared view, which is what the earlier chapters called a global section, is a choice of one number xv per town such that on every road the two translated numbers agree: aexu=bexvfor every road e=(u→v).aexu=bexvfor every road e=(u→v). Chapters 1 to 3 took every ae and be equal to 1. That case is the constant sheaf, the mathematics of everyone looking at the same thing. Now the maps can be anything, and I call a pair of such maps on a road a frame: it is how the two ends render what they hold into terms the other can take in.

Walk around and see what a shared view demands. Take a=(1,1,1) and b=(2,1,12). Road 1 says xA=2xB, so if Alder holds 1, Birch holds 12. Road 2 says xC=xB, so Cedar holds 12. Road 3 says 12xA=xC, and 12=12. The loop closes, and the shared view is (1,12,12) up to scale. The three towns do not hold the same number, and they agree. A visitor from the hill reading the raw numbers would report a disagreement where there is none; agreement here means equal after translation.

Now take a=(1,1,1) and b=(1,1,2). Road 1: xB=xA. Road 2: xC=xB. Road 3: 2xA=xC. Together these say 2xA=xA, which only zero satisfies. Alder and Birch can agree, Birch and Cedar can agree, and Cedar and Alder can agree, and the three together can agree on nothing.

The rule, and the matrix behind it

Write the three conditions as one matrix equation Dx=0 with D=(−a1−b1−0−0−a2−b2−b3−0−a3),detD=b1b2b3−a1a2a3.D=(−a1−b1−0−0−a2−b2−b3−0−a3),detD=b1b2b3−a1a2a3. A nonzero shared view exists exactly when detD=0, which is the condition ρ1ρ2ρ3=1,ρe=aebe.ρ1ρ2ρ3=1,ρe=aebe. Road by road, xv=ρexu: the number ρe is what a view at u becomes when carried across the road to v. The product of the three, the holonomy of the loop, is what a view becomes after one trip around. The frames compose when that is the identity. In the first example the holonomy is 12×1×2=1 and in the second it is 1×1×12=12.

If you prefer cohomology: D is the coboundary map from the stalks on the towns to the spaces on the roads, H0=ker⁡D is the set of shared views and H1=cokerD. Because D is square here, dim⁡H0=dim⁡H1 whatever the frames are. Flat frames give one dimension each. The frames that do not compose give zero each, and that is the odd feature of this example: the obstruction is not a large H1 but a collapsed H0. Nothing that comes in from the roads is left unexplained, and nothing at all survives as a shared view.

Two kinds of failure

Chapter 3 tested whether reported gaps fitted a model of price levels. There the model was fine and the reports could be wrong, a specification the data may reject. Here no report has been mentioned. The machine itself guarantees that nothing nonzero can be held in common, before anyone looks. In an econometrician’s terms the first is a specification rejected by the data and the second is a specification whose restrictions contradict one another. Better measurement can in principle fix the first. It cannot fix the second, because the second is not about measurement.

4.3Logarithms, holonomy and the loop test

Take logarithms of the carrying factors: ℓe=log⁡ρe. Then the holonomy is 1 exactly when ℓ1+ℓ2+ℓ3=0. A product has become a sum, and the question has become one already familiar. On a graph with numbers ℓe on its edges, the sum around every loop vanishes exactly when there are numbers gv at the nodes with ℓe=gv−gu on every edge, which is to say when ℓ is a gradient. On the triangle, gv=log⁡xv, and the shared view is the potential. Such a flow is called a coboundary, and Chapter 3 built a test for the part of an observed flow that is not one. On a graph with more loops the condition is the same around each loop of a cycle basis, E−V+1 of them, and the multiplicative frames compose if and only if log⁡ρ is a coboundary.

Figure 4.3 shows what the sum is doing, with the logarithm as the vertical axis. Stand the triangle on a circle and let the height record the logarithm of the number held. Walking a road moves you up or down by ℓe. With the flat frames b=(2,1,12) the heights are 0, −1, −1 and back to 0, so the path is a closed loop. With b=(1,1,2) the heights are 0, 0, 0 and then −1 on the last road, so after one lap you are standing on the level below the one you left, and after two laps two levels below. The ramp is the holonomy made visible: each lap is a local success and the total is a drop. Neither picture contains any noise. A different way to see the same thing is that the circle has no consistent height function, in the way a spiral staircase has none.

What you can and cannot see

Suppose each town changes its unit, writing xv′=gvxv with gv>0. Then ρe becomes ρegv/gu on road e=(u→v), and in logs ℓe changes by the gradient log⁡gv−log⁡gu. The holonomy around a loop does not change at all, because the g’s cancel as you go around. So two sets of frames that differ by a change of units describe the same situation, and the holonomies are what survive. Physicists call a change of units of this kind a gauge change.

Two consequences follow, and they are worth stating plainly. First, on a tree every set of frames composes. Fix the number at one town and carry it outward; no road ever returns to a town already visited, so nothing can contradict it. Second, a difference in units between two places cannot be told from the physical situation by comparing numbers along a tree. A loop is needed, and what it reveals is only the product around it. This is the same fact as Chapter 3’s finding that on a tree the residual is identically zero, and that on a single ring a nonzero residual can be detected and not located. If the factors on the ring are ℓe and the only information is the sum, nothing singles out one road as the wrong one. That fact is about to decide how a piano gets tuned.

Two remarks on generality. If the factors may be negative the same condition holds with the sign included, and a holonomy of −1 is the signed case: a network of friends and enemies has a loop that fails when the number of enemy links on it is odd. That special case is a known theorem, as the first book observed. And if the stalks have more than one dimension the factors are matrices, their order matters, and the holonomy is defined only up to the choice of starting point; I will not need that in this book.

One road too many

A one-line fact about this machine deserves a place, because the first book made much of its moral. Adding a road adds a row to D, and a vector that satisfies the larger system satisfies the smaller one. So the space of shared views can stay the same or shrink; it can never grow. Take the frames b=(1,1,2) again and let Cedar and Alder not yet trade. The towns form a line, and the shared view (1,1,1) meets both demands. Build the road from Cedar to Alder, and the view is gone. More connection destroyed an agreement that was there. We had this as a headline in the research notes and removed it: it is a one-line consequence of the algebra, and the signed-network case is known. I keep it here as a picture of how a loop is where the latent trouble in the frames finds somewhere to show up.

4.4Three loops that do not close

The arithmetic of the last section applies unchanged to the three loops that opened the chapter. The table lists what plays each part; the pages after it say what each loop does with its miss.

Piano Magellan’s ship Exchange rates (invented)
A place a note a longitude a currency
A local step one pure fifth, ×32 one counted day, +1 one quoted rate
What accumulates positive ratios; cents add integers; days add positive ratios; logs add
Holonomy 312/219=1.01364, or 23.46 cents −1 day 1.071
Where the miss goes into the fifths, or onto one wolf fifth onto a chosen meridian, the date line to whoever trades the loop, or into the quotes

The piano

If the miss cannot be removed, it can be put somewhere. Each way of tuning the twelve fifths is a list of twelve errors ek, the number of cents by which fifth k falls short of or exceeds 701.955, and the circle closes exactly when the errors sum to −23.46. That sum is the holonomy and every tuning has to meet it. Three ways of meeting it are in Figure 4.4.

The first leaves eleven fifths pure and puts the whole comma on the twelfth, which becomes the wolf fifth, 678.49 cents and unmistakably wrong. The second is the tuning of the instrument on which most of us have played: the comma is shared equally, every fifth is 1.955 cents flat, every fifth is 700 cents, and no key is better or worse than another. The third, quarter-comma meantone, makes up its mind about something else. A major third is four fifths up less two octaves, and it is a pure 5:4, 386.31 cents, exactly when the fifth is 51/4, 696.58 cents, which is 5.38 cents flat. Eleven fifths take that value and the twelfth takes up the rest: 737.64 cents, 35.68 cents wider than a pure fifth. The sum is again −23.46.

The price of each choice shows up in the major thirds. With a wolf and eleven pure fifths, eight of the twelve thirds are the old Pythagorean third, 407.82 cents, which is 21.51 cents wider than a pure 5:4; the other four, which span the wolf, are 1.95 cents narrow. In equal temperament every third is 400 cents, 13.69 cents wide of pure. In meantone eight thirds are pure and the four that span the wolf are 41.06 cents wide. Nobody gets everything. The computation behind those figures is in figures/ch04_numbers.py, and Figure 4.4 lets you move the comma around yourself.

Why is the equal division the one on the piano? Here is the argument, and it is the argument of Chapter 3. Ask for errors e1,…,e12 that close the circle, ∑ek=−c with c=23.46, and make them as small as possible in the least-squares sense. Lagrange gives 2ek=λ for every k, so all errors are equal, ek=−c/12=−1.955. The sum of squares is 45.9 for equal temperament, 550.4 for the wolf tuning and 1591.2 for quarter-comma meantone. If some keys matter more than others, weight them: minimizing ∑wkek2 under the same constraint gives errors proportional to 1/wk, so a key you play often takes a smaller share of the comma. Meantone is not least squares at all; it optimizes a different set of intervals, the thirds, and pays for it with a wolf. A ring that has one loop cannot say which edge is wrong, so the choice of where to put the miss is the tuner’s and not the data’s.

There is a second loop under the first, and meantone found it. Four pure fifths up, less two octaves, is 81/64, and the pure third is 5/4. They differ by 81/80, the syntonic comma, 21.51 cents. Three pure thirds fall short of an octave by 41.06 cents (128/125). The three miss-sizes are tied together: 3×21.51−23.46=41.06. If pure octaves, pure fifths and pure thirds were all to hold, these loops would have to close at once, and they cannot: 1, log2⁡3 and log2⁡5 are linearly independent over the rationals, because 3m5n=2k has no solution beyond m=n=k=0.

Magellan’s missing day

In July 1522 the one surviving ship of Magellan’s expedition, having sailed west around the world, put in at the Cape Verde Islands. The crew had kept a careful log for three years, with a day recorded for every sunrise, and asked the people ashore what day it was. They were told Thursday. The log said Wednesday. The story comes from the first book; nothing in the reading for this project checks the details, so treat it as an illustration and not as a citation.

No one had miscounted. Sailing west the crew had chased the sun, each day from sunrise to sunrise a little longer than twenty-four hours, and around the whole circle they had met one sunrise fewer than a stay-at-home. Every local step was right and the total is off by one. This is a loop whose carried quantity is an integer, a count of days, instead of a positive ratio. The group is additive from the start, so no logarithm is needed, and the holonomy is −1.

What does the world do with this miss? It does what the wolf fifth does. We put it in one place. The International Date Line is a chosen curve across the Pacific where the calendar jumps by a day, so that everywhere else a trip of a few hundred kilometers changes nothing. Moving the line moves the jump and cannot delete it, and moving it is the gauge change of the last section. The piano gave us three placements of the same loop sum; the calendar chose the one in which the entire miss sits on a single edge.

Exchange rates

Now money. Here are three quotes I have invented, so the numbers carry no information about any market: US dollars to euros at 0.90, euros to pounds at 0.85, pounds to dollars at 1.40. Start with 100 dollars. After the first conversion you hold 90.00 euros, after the second 76.50 pounds and after the third 107.10 dollars (Figure 4.5). Each quote is internally unobjectionable, and three of them in a triangle return 7.1 percent for nothing, the product 0.90×0.85×1.40=1.071. The loop in the opposite direction returns 1/1.071 of what you put in, so only one direction pays. That product is the holonomy, and there is no arbitrage exactly when it is 1: that is the no-arbitrage condition, and it is the condition for the exchange rates to compose as frames.

In logs the three rates are −0.1054, −0.1625 and 0.3365, summing to 0.0686=log⁡1.071. A set of quotes is arbitrage-free when this log flow has no circulation, which is the question Chapter 3 answered for edge flows. If the quotes were noisy readings of a consistent set and you wanted the closest consistent set in the least-squares sense, you would divide the log miss equally among the three edges, as the piano tuner did. Each rate is multiplied by 1.071−1/3=0.9774, giving 0.8797, 0.8308 and 1.3684, whose product is 1.

Two cautions. First, the miss is large enough to be seen here because I chose it, and real quotes are kept much closer to consistent by people who trade the loop. Second, conversions cost something. If each conversion hands over a fraction c in fees, the round trip multiplies by 1.071(1−c)3, and the loop pays only when c<1−1.071−1/3=2.26 percent. The band of quotes that cannot be traded is thus the analogue of the band of Chapter 8: a loop need not close exactly to be consistent with the observed frictions. We derived that bound here for the example. It is not from a source.

4.5Why we will need this later

Three links, in order of how firm they are.

The first is firm. A loop can fail because the data do not fit a model that could fit, or because the model is incapable of fitting. Chapter 3 is the first and this chapter is the second. In Chapters 8 and 9 there will be a third kind of failure that is neither: tables of probabilities that each agree on what they share and have no common joint distribution. Abramsky and Brandenburger show that there the linear equations always have a solution over the reals, with negative weights allowed, and the whole obstruction is the requirement that probabilities be non-negative. So the failure there is an inequality and the failure in this chapter is an equation. Keeping the two apart prevents a good deal of confusion.

The second is an identification point, written in the memo and developed there for surveys: a difference in how a shared variable is measured and a failure to cohere cannot be told apart without assuming a rule for comparing the two measurements. In this chapter the statement has a precise form. The carrying factors ρe are the rule. On a tree no data can reveal them, because every set of factors is a change of units; on a loop only the product is revealed. Anyone who reports a failure to glue has already adopted a ρ, and a different ρ can give a different verdict.

The third is a question, and we do not know the answer. In the contextuality-by-default program of Dzhafarov, Kujala and coauthors, the same property measured in two contexts counts as two different random variables, and one compares them through a rule, the maximal coupling, which their papers present as one choice among many. A restriction map that is not the identity does the same job in the linear setting: it is a stated rule for comparing what two places hold. It is natural to ask whether contextuality-by-default corresponds exactly to sheaves with restriction maps other than the identity. The memo lists as still to do a check of whether anyone has written that correspondence down, and the check has not been made. What this chapter provides is the linear case, in which the rule is a number on each end of a road and the holonomy is a product. Chapter 11 takes up the probabilistic case.

4.6What the papers say

What the paper says: Hansen and Ghrist (2021), “Opinion dynamics on discourse sheaves”

Read in full except the proofs. Each person has a space of opinions and each conversation a space of expressions, linked by restriction maps; two people can express the same thing without holding the same opinion, which is exactly the situation of the first example above. They show that diffusion of opinions converges to the orthogonal projection of the starting opinions onto the global sections, and that when there are none beyond zero the only stable opinions are zero. That is the second example of this chapter put into motion. Their Theorem 9 gives an identification condition: if no nonzero global section vanishes on a set of people, the dynamics observed on that set are detectable, so watching them recovers the part of everyone’s state that lies in the global sections. Their Theorem 11 lets the maps move so as to fit the opinions, a model of frame revision. The paper has no prices, no markets and, in the passages we read, no statistics, so whether a log-ratio test of the kind in Chapter 3 applies to it is not something it addresses.

What the paper says: Bosca and Ghrist (2026), “Selective adaptation of beliefs and communication on cellular sheaves”

Read for dissection in arXiv version 2: the abstract, introduction and conclusion in full and the statement of every result in Sections 3 to 6; the proofs and appendices were not read. The paper lets people change how they talk instead of what they believe, makes stubbornness directional, and gives a conservation law that forbids agreement by collapse to zero, for vertices all of whose channels adapt. It names evolving stalks, meaning opinion spaces that themselves change, as an open problem. That is the objection about inherited frames in its strongest form, and the authors leave it open.

What the paper says: Biesel, McSwiggen, Theodosopoulos and Titelbaum (2025), “Topological obstructions to shared priors”

Read for dissection: pages 1 to 8, the statements of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 and the closing section; the cohomology background and the proofs were not read. Agents are aware of different sets of possibilities and hold a probability on their own set. They ask when one prior over the whole space has each agent’s measure as its conditional. For agents who are pairwise compatible, the log ratio log⁡Pi(B)/Pj(B) is a one-cocycle, and Theorem 4.1 says it is a coboundary exactly when a common prior exists. That is the logarithmic step of this chapter in a probabilistic setting. Theorem 4.2 says pairwise checks suffice for every configuration if and only if the overlap complex has no first cohomology. We tried to map this onto the spending-share correction in the next section; the mapping is exact for the cocycle but the paper’s hypothesis, that agents are pairwise compatible, requires identical relative shares on common goods, and with prices that differ across countries that fails generically. So their theorem does not apply to our experiment as stated.

What the paper says: Abramsky and Brandenburger (2011), “The sheaf-theoretic structure of non-locality and contextuality”

Read for dissection, arXiv version 7: the introduction in full and the statement of every main theorem, not the proofs. Measurements are questions, a context is a set of questions asked together, and an empirical model gives one distribution per context. A global section is a joint distribution behind all of them. The claim used above is theirs: over the reals the linear system always has a solution for a compatible family, and everything rests on non-negativity. In what we read, the paper uses no scalar restriction maps other than the identity.

What the paper says: Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson (2015); Dzhafarov and Kujala (2016); Dzhafarov, Zhang and Kujala (2016)

The first is read in full in its main text. A property measured in context c is a random variable Rc, and the same property in another context is a different variable with no joint distribution with the first. If the copies have different distributions, no joint can make them equal, so the authors ask for a joint in which copies are equal as often as their distributions allow, a maximal coupling. For a cycle of two-valued properties they give a necessary and sufficient inequality, and with consistent margins it reduces to the Leggett–Garg inequality for three properties, the CHSH inequality for four and the KCBS inequality for five. For three with uniform margins it is the triangle inequality of Chapter 8; we checked that numerically. Dzhafarov and Kujala (2016) we read in the conclusion only. It says whether a system is contextual depends on a classification into contents and contexts made before the theory applies, and that maximal coupling is one rule among many. Dzhafarov, Zhang and Kujala (2016), abstract and conclusion only, review behavioral and social data and report none that provides evidence for contextuality, reading every apparent context effect as a direct influence on a margin. We have not read its body or any later challenge.

What the paper says: Group synchronization (Singer 2011; Lerman and Shi); King, Murray, Salomon and Tandon (2004)

Both read as summaries only, so these are leads and not findings. Group synchronization recovers group elements from noisy pairwise ratios, with the product of ratios around a cycle required to be the identity; that is the non-abelian version of this chapter, and an estimate of which edges are corrupted can be made from cycle inconsistencies. King and coauthors measure how different groups of survey respondents use a response scale by anchoring each group to common vignettes. Anchoring every group to one reference is a star, which is a tree, so by the argument above their frames always compose and no loop exists to test them. Whether anyone has noted that We did not check.

What the paper says: Feenstra (1994); Handbury and Weinstein (2015)

Feenstra’s paper was not read in this project; it is cited for the variety adjustment that Chapter 7 will use. Handbury and Weinstein were read for dissection in the published version, the introduction in full and Sections 2 to 6 selectively. Both enter below only through the share λ that corrects a comparison on shared goods.

The music is not in any paper we read. The piano figures are standard arithmetic that we computed, and the Magellan story is the first book’s.

4.7What we found

Two of the research cycles reached this chapter.

Cycle 1 turned the loop sum into a test and checked its size. On ten nodes with a ring and five chords, 4000 replications and noise of 0.05 on the log scale, the chi-squared test on the log-transformed frames rejected a true null at the 5 percent level in 5.4 percent of runs. The Monte Carlo standard error at that size is 0.34 percentage points, so 5.4 is about 1.2 standard errors above nominal. That is the sense in which the same test applies in logs. The cycle also found that on a tree the residual is zero and nothing can be tested, and that, in the additive version of the experiment, on a ring of ten a real shift of 0.5 on one edge was located correctly 9.2 percent of the time against 10 percent by chance. The ring cannot say which conversion is wrong, which is the piano tuner’s problem. The cycle’s own verdict was that the test is correct and not new: its parts are standard in geodesy, psychometrics and group synchronization.

Cycle 3 is where frames meet economics. Eight countries consume their own subsets of forty goods, and two countries can be compared only on the goods they share. The matched index is Sato–Vartia on the shared goods with shares renormalized there; in the language of this chapter its restriction map is projection onto the shared goods. The corrected index adds Feenstra’s variety adjustment, (log⁡λk−log⁡λj)/(σ−1), where λc is the share of country c’s spending that falls on the shared goods. We checked that, in every one of 200 economies per cell, the corrected index equaled the true difference in price levels plus the taste term on the shared goods, to 3×10−13. The entries below are the share of each index’s variation that does not glue (σ=4; q is the chance that a country consumes a given good):

Identical tastes Taste dispersion 0.2
q Mean overlap Matched Corrected Matched Corrected
1.0 100% 0.0% 0.0% 0.9% 0.9%
0.8 67% 19.4% 0.0% 19.1% 1.9%
0.6 43% 35.3% 0.0% 36.0% 2.9%
0.4 26% 49.1% 0.0% 46.8% 4.7%

With the projection as the restriction map, a fifth of the variation fails to glue at two thirds overlap and half at a quarter overlap, with identical tastes, so nothing economic is wrong. With the λ correction the comparison glues exactly under identical tastes at every overlap, and with taste differences what remains is the taste term, growing from 0.9 to 4.7 percent as overlap falls. The λ are one number per country per road, the multiplicative frames of this chapter, and under identical tastes they compose around every loop. So projection was the wrong restriction map and the right one carries a frame.

The corrections made along the way are the part worth not skipping.

  • Cycle 2, the experiment before this one, gave every country the same goods and so tested only the constant sheaf. Cycle 3 exists because that left out the feature of the framework that distinguishes it, countries with different stalks.

  • The result is Feenstra’s variety adjustment, carried from time to space, and Handbury and Weinstein apply it across cities. The sheaf reading is for now a restatement; it would be more if it produced a test of which pairs’ variety terms disagree, or a rule for which bilateral comparisons to collect, and it has not.

  • In cycle 2 we read taste shifters as frames. They are not: a taste shifter is a preference parameter, and the frame of the first book was how a person renders what they hold into shared terms. The λ factors are the real economic instance, and the taste term is the part of the obstruction that stays.

  • The experiment assumes constant elasticity of substitution with one known σ. The correction is sensitive to σ, and the taste obstruction stays under 5 percent in the cells we ran.

  • The headline “adding a link can destroy agreement” was dropped, as above.

The memo’s identification point was written later, after reading Dzhafarov and Kujala. It rests on the survey simulations of cycles 7 and 8, which Chapter 11 reports, and no experiment in this chapter’s cycles tests it on frames. The open question about restriction maps and contextuality-by-default is also still open. Chapter 11 starts from it.

Try it

Try it 4.1. Let a=(2,1,3) and b=(1,4,b3). For what b3 do the frames compose? For that value, find the shared view with xA=1, and check road 3.

Try it 4.2. Show that rescaling town v’s unit by gv changes ρe by gv/gu and leaves the holonomy around every loop unchanged. Use it to show that on a path of towns any set of positive frames composes, and say what comparisons of numbers alone can and cannot identify about the frames.

Try it 4.3. Minimizing ∑kwkek2 subject to ∑kek=−c gives ek=−c/(wk∑j1/wj). Derive it. Then give one fifth a weight ten times the others and say how much of the comma each fifth takes.

Try it 4.4. With the quotes 0.90, 0.85 and 1.40, find the profit from a trip around the loop in the other direction, and find the proportional fee at which the profitable direction stops paying. Then replace each quote by its equal-log repair and confirm that the product is one.
